title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Dream

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel, and arguably his strangest, richest, most unnerving masterpiece.
Each week we take a set of passages and ask: what is Dickens actually doing here?
Not what the story is, but how it works — the machinery beneath the surface.
Today we open with the novel's central obsession: dust, money, and the vast theatre of human appetite that surrounds sudden wealth.
I have three brilliant companions with me, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — every gear matters.
She will be our guide to the craft: the sentences, the images, the architecture of the prose.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's deepest subject is always individual character under pressure — not society, but the soul.
He keeps the rest of us honest when we're tempted to turn Dickens into a pamphlet.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — who extracts value from whom, and how the system conceals the fact.
He is, in the best possible sense, Dickens's most demanding reader.
Our passages today give us Boffin — the Golden Dustman — suddenly rich and immediately besieged.
Eleanor, let's begin with you.
What strikes me first about these passages is the sheer structural audacity of the catalogue form Dickens deploys here.
He doesn't describe charity corruption once — he lists it, enumerates it, overwhelms you with it.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — the accumulation itself becomes the argument.
And then, right at the apex of this avalanche, Dickens drops in the Duke of Linseed's letter.
The setup is simply this:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Four adjectives before the noun — and every one of them does damage.
"Large" — self-important. "Fat" — glutted with its own consequence. "Private" — the fraudulent intimacy of the mass-produced appeal.
The ducal coronet seals not just the letter but the argument: rank is the final, brazen credential of the beggar.
Eleanor is right to admire the craft, and I do admire it — though I'd resist the temptation to read it purely as social anatomy.
What Dickens is satirising here is something older and more permanent than any particular class arrangement.
It is cupidity — simple, ancient, unkillable human cupidity — dressed in the costume of benevolence.
The Duke of Linseed is not a symptom of capitalism. He is a figure of moral comedy as old as Jonson's Volpone.
What is delicious is the postscript — "the Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas" — which Dickens calls, with perfect irony, "thoughtful."
The narrator's mock-admiration is where the real blade is hidden.
This is Dickens as moralist, not as political economist — and the distinction matters.
I take Edmund's point about cupidity — but I think Dickens is doing something more precise than timeless moral comedy.
Look at the individual beggars in the very next passage — the catalogue that follows the ducal letter.
Dickens gives us a taxonomy of desperation — officers' daughters, secretive wives, husbands, the inspired, the independent.
And then he delivers this extraordinary aside about their documents:
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is brutal in exactly the right way — the process of reduction is the point.
A calf becomes minced veal — a living creature processed into a commodity.
These people's entire histories — their evidence of suffering — have been ground down into scraps that the system will not recognise.
Edmund calls it moral comedy. I call it a precise account of what poverty actually does to a person's legibility in the world.
Daniel's reading of that simile is exactly right — and it connects to something structural that runs through all three of these passages.
We have the great Dust Mound — Harmon's fortune — at the centre of everything.
And Wegg's revelation of the later will tells us something devastating about what that fortune actually meant to its original creator.
Wegg reads the will, and the terms are almost comically sparse:

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Quite enough for him" — that is perhaps the most corrosive phrase in the whole novel.
Old Harmon couldn't even bring himself to bequeath — he could only withhold, dismiss, and punish from beyond the grave.
Eleanor has put her finger on something that I think is the novel's deepest subject — and it isn't, with respect to Daniel, the mechanics of economic extraction.
It is the question of what a man does with his freedom — and what happens when freedom arrives unearned, unasked for, in the form of dust and gold.
Boffin is a man of genuine goodness suddenly placed at the centre of a vortex of appetite.
The whole machinery of begging — ducal and destitute alike — is a test of character, not merely a portrait of a corrupt economy.
That is what Dickens understood, and what he never let his satirical energy quite obscure.
I won't quarrel with the idea of character being tested — but tested by what, and why, and at whose expense?
The beggars on horseback — those who need a clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope to complete their road to affluence — are grotesque, yes.
But Dickens also gives us the woman partaking of a cold potato by a flickering lucifer-match, with a heartless landlady threatening to throw her into the streets like a dog.
The satirical catalogue doesn't flatten those people — it holds them in tension with the farcical ones.
And that tension is what makes Dickens something more than a moralist — he is a novelist who refuses to let the comedy cancel the suffering.
Character under pressure, the legibility of the poor, the architecture of satirical prose — we've already staked out the three territories this novel will keep pulling us back to.
And sitting at the centre of all of it: the Dust Heaps, the fortune built from London's refuse, and one good-natured man trying to navigate the storm it has conjured.
We'll go deeper into that storm after the break.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, carefully, to see how it works and what it means.
Today's segment sits at the heart of the book — money, morality, and one young woman's reckoning with both.
We're calling it Bella's Bargain.
With me today are three exceptional guides to this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a fine mechanism — always asking how the thing is built.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists that the truest subject of any great novel is the moral life of individual human beings under pressure.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who asks, always, whose interests a novel's world serves — and whose it destroys.
The question before us: what does Our Mutual Friend actually say about money — and can Bella Wilfer escape it?
What strikes me first about Bella's arc in these chapters is how Dickens structures guilt and desire simultaneously within the same character.
Bella wants money — she says so openly, almost defiantly — and yet the novel refuses to make that wanting simply wicked.
What Rokesmith's long interior monologue reveals is how profoundly money has already corrupted the terms on which any relationship between these two people could be formed.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary passage where Rokesmith thinks through the impossible trap he is caught in.
"Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?"
That syntactical balance — shame on one side, meanness on the other — is Dickens at his most geometrically precise.
There is no honourable move available to him — and that is money's doing, not anyone's bad character.
Eleanor makes the structural observation elegantly, but I want to pause on something she perhaps glides past — the phrase "moral timidity that dates from my childhood."
Dickens is not simply indicting a system here.
He is tracing the formation of a particular character — a man whose capacity for moral courage has been stunted by a loveless upbringing.
Rokesmith tells us, in his own voice, why he devised this elaborate fiction.

"The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil — was strong upon the moral timidity that dates from my childhood with my poor sister."
This is the confession of a wounded man, not a critique of capital.
The pathos belongs to the individual soul — which is, I would submit, precisely where Dickens intended it.
Edmund, I admire the reading, and the wounded-man framing is genuinely moving — but I think it does exactly what the ideology of the text wants us to do.
It privatises a structural problem — makes it a matter of one family's psychological damage, rather than asking what kind of economy produces fathers like John Harmon senior.
Dickens himself supplies the answer, and it is not flattering to the system.
Notice the phrase Rokesmith uses — and it is extraordinary: "the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence."
"the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence"
All within their influence — not just one son, not just the family.
Wealth radiates harm outward like a contagion — and Dickens knows it, even if his resolution tries to contain that knowledge within a love story.
Daniel's point about contagion is exactly right, and it connects to something Dickens does in the Lizzie passages that I find quietly devastating.
There's a moment where Lizzie describes a child — not Bella, but a figure who casts a shadow over everything the novel says about what poverty actually manufactures.
The line is simple, almost plain, and it lands like a blow.
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
That parenthesis — "if she ever had one" — is almost unbearable.
Dickens reaches past the metaphor of poverty and makes it brutally, bodily concrete — a cradle that may never have existed.
And the craft point is this: that parenthesis is doing more moral work than a page of editorial commentary could.
That parenthesis is indeed extraordinary — and I shan't quarrel with Eleanor on the craft.
What I would insist on is that Lizzie's charity here — her knowledge of this child, her compassion — is itself a moral act, not a structural symptom.
Dickens is quite clear that the child's father is, and I quote, "a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober — but a good workman too, at the work he does."
That qualification — "a good workman too" — is the novelist's essential generosity.
Dickens will not let the wretched become merely emblematic.
Each ruined life retains a residue of dignity — which is a moral claim, not an economic one.
Edmund's point about dignity is well taken — and I don't dismiss it.
But I want to bring in Boffin's speech about charitable patronage, because it shows Dickens working on a different register entirely — satirical, almost savage.
This is Dickens anatomising the philanthropic industry — the way charity becomes a mechanism for self-aggrandisement rather than relief.
Boffin names it with magnificent contempt.

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The list proliferates until it becomes absurd — and that absurdity is the point.
The charity apparatus doesn't relieve suffering — it produces titles, hierarchies, the performance of benevolence.
And Rokesmith sits at the centre of it, up to his neck — which is also, of course, his position throughout the entire novel.
That image of Rokesmith drowning in charity paperwork is almost comic — and yet Dickens makes sure we feel the suffocation.
Which brings me to the Wegg and Venus scene — because Dickens gives us another version of the money-swoon, and this time entirely farcical.
Wegg's wooden leg rises as the excitement mounts, he topples against Venus, and Dickens gives us this perfectly judged phrase.
"both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon."
"Pecuniary swoon" — two words that do everything: comic, precise, and quietly damning.
Money, Dickens is saying, produces a kind of derangement — not just in the wretched and the villainous, but in everyone it touches.
The Wegg scene is pure comic genius, and I would not have it otherwise.
But I think Eleanor and Daniel both risk over-systematising what is, at its best, a novelist's free and exuberant imagination.
Wegg is not an emblem of capitalism — he is a magnificently realised rogue, greedy in the particular way that only Wegg can be greedy.
The wooden leg rising of its own accord — the body betraying the will's pretences — that is the comedy of human self-deception, not of political economy.
Dickens is always funnier, and always more humane, than any single reading can quite contain.
Edmund, I'll grant you Wegg's magnificent particularity — and I'll even grant you that no single reading contains Dickens entirely.

But notice what Rokesmith's confession ultimately forces us to confront — that the entire architecture of the plot, the disguise, the test, the deception, is generated by the corrupting power of inherited money.
Rokesmith himself says he conceived his deception because of "the misery-making money" — those three words, packed together, are Dickens's verdict.
"This is another of the old perverted uses of the misery-making money."
"Old" and "perverted" — this is not a new aberration but the system's normal operation.
Bella's transformation is real and it is moving — but it takes place inside a world where the money never goes away.
And that tension — between individual redemption and systemic constraint — may be precisely where the novel's power resides.
Bella wanting money, Rokesmith drowning in its consequences, Wegg swooning at the prospect of it — Dickens keeps returning to the same gravitational centre.
In our next segment, we'll follow that money further downstream — into the river, the dust heaps, and the institutions that profit from both.

segments.title: Telling and Hiding: Narrative Masks in Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the series where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart scene by scene.
I'm joined today by three voices whose disagreements are, honestly, as illuminating as their agreements.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — for the engineering behind the beauty.
Sir Edmund Leigh spent decades at Oxford reading novels as moral documents, and he is not easily impressed by fashionable interpretations.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen brings the historian's eye — he wants to know who holds power, who pays for it, and what the novel knows about both questions.
Today's segment is called Telling and Hiding: Narrative Masks in Our Mutual Friend.
We're looking at the novel's deep interest in concealment — characters who hide what they know, narrators who perform revelation, villains who mistake their own cunning for intelligence.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with a passage that is, on the surface, a villains' planning meeting, but is really something far stranger.
Thank you — and yes, the Wegg and Venus scene is extraordinary, because Dickens doesn't simply report villainy, he performs it in the very syntax of the narration.
Wegg's scheme is rendered in a kind of parliamentary parody — all those 'That's and sub-clauses, as though extortion were being moved as a motion in committee.
The cumulative effect is devastating satire — Dickens is mocking the procedural language of property and contract by placing it in the mouth of a man planning blackmail.
And then Dickens gives Wegg his thesis statement — listen to how precisely it is phrased:
'he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
'Halves!' — one word that compresses greed, partnership, and total moral vacancy into a single exclamation.
And it gets darker — there's also the threat of what Dickens calls 'abject moral bondage and slavery' if Boffin steps out of line.
The word 'slavery' is not an accident in a novel so saturated with economic subjugation — Dickens knows exactly what he is saying.
Eleanor is absolutely right that the language is doing political work here — but I want to push further.
Wegg's scheme is not a perversion of the property system — it is a perfect imitation of it.
Find a document that gives you leverage. Hold it over someone with less power. Extract half their wealth or more. That is investment law in 1865.
What makes Wegg comic — and Dickens is always doing this — is that he is a small man performing the logic of large men.
And notice the phrase: the plan involves letting Boffin bear 'the trouble and cost of daily digging' while Wegg profits from the disturbance.
'They should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away... while they might nightly turn such complete disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations.'
One man's labour, another man's gain — that is the fundamental mechanism, rendered here in miniature and in farce.
I find myself in the uncomfortable position of agreeing with both of you, while wanting to add a complication.
What Dickens is anatomising in Wegg is not simply avarice — it is self-deception of a particular English variety.
Wegg genuinely believes, one suspects, that the word 'Halves' is a reasonable, even magnanimous, settlement.
His offer to be corrected if Two-thirds or Three-fourths were more just is the detail that kills me — it is self-righteousness masquerading as flexibility.
And this connects, for me, to the Boffins themselves — because what makes them remarkable is precisely the absence of that self-deception.

When Mr Boffin describes standing up for young John Harmon against old Harmon's brutality, there is no rhetoric, no self-congratulation — only the bare facts, rendered with the man's own plain speech.
Dickens gives us the bonnet detail — and it is a detail worthy of Johnson's praise for the particular over the general:
'she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head.'
That parenthetical portrait of Mrs Boffin's hat is Dickens asserting that virtue is not abstract — it wears a bonnet.
Edmund, that parenthetical is doing so much structural work — I am glad you landed on it.
It's a digression that isn't a digression — it anchors the whole scene in the physical world so that the violence that follows lands with real weight.
And then the short, percussive sentence at the end — 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.' — that repetition is extraordinary.
'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
The second 'Dropped her' is not emphasis for its own sake — it is Boffin's voice breaking slightly under the memory, the sentence collapsing under the weight of the image.
Dickens is writing a man who cannot quite finish the story — and so the narration itself becomes a performance of grief.
What strikes me about that passage — and Eleanor's reading deepens this — is the context in which Boffin is telling it.
He is explaining to Lightwood why the inheritance is, in some profound sense, already tainted — already paid for in suffering before a penny changed hands.
The poor boy 'gets no good of it' — he is lifted toward the cup and killed before he drinks.
And here the narrator's account of old Harmon's will becomes almost unbearably cold — the dead man trusted the Boffins precisely because he knew his wealth could not buy them.
Dickens puts it this way:
'he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt.'
That word 'powerlessness' applied to wealth is the novel's central paradox — and Dickens earns it by showing us, one bonnet at a time, exactly what incorruptibility looks like from the inside.
Daniel, I think that is the passage that vindicates my view of the novel's moral centre entirely — though I suspect you arrived there by a rather different road.
Old Harmon is, in every sense, a figure of complete worldly corruption — and yet even in his corruption he recognises goodness when he sees it.
Dickens names him the 'dead Jailer of Harmony Jail' — which is one of those compound epithets that arrives fully loaded with irony and sorrow at once.
And his recognising the Boffins' integrity while simultaneously raging at them for it — that is the authentic grammar of self-contempt.
The man 'mistrusted all mankind — and sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself.'
Dickens understood that the worst misanthropes are self-haters, and he gives that understanding to his narrator with the lightest, most devastating touch.
I want to bring in a very different kind of self-knowledge before we close — or rather, its absence.
There is a small moment between Eugene Wrayburn and Mortimer Lightwood that I find almost unbearably precise as a study in a man who genuinely cannot read himself.
Lightwood tells him to look ahead, to plan — and Eugene catches the phrase and turns it back immediately:
'That's exactly what I am incapable of doing.'
What the narrator adds is the key — Eugene says this 'gaily,' but also 'with a perplexed and inquisitive face, as if he actually did not know what to make of himself.'
The mask of wit is worn so long it has become the face — and the face beneath it is genuinely confused.
That is Dickens at his finest — a character who performs self-knowledge, and in that very performance reveals how little of it he actually possesses.
That image of the mask becoming the face is, I think, the thread that ties this entire segment together.
From Wegg's self-deluding proceduralism to old Harmon's bitter self-recognition, from Mrs Boffin's hat to Eugene's performed irony — the novel keeps asking who in this story actually sees clearly.
Eleanor, Edmund, Daniel — thank you.
We'll continue in our next segment, where we turn to the river — what it takes, what it gives back, and what it knows.

segments.title: The Thames and the City: Setting as Social Commentary

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep on one of the great pleasures of this novel — Dickens as a writer of place.
Not just the Thames — though we'll get there — but every room, every institution, every dinner table that Dickens gives us.
Our guide through this territory today is Dr Daniel Rosen, a cultural historian who reads settings in fiction as social documents — blueprints of how power actually works.
We're also joined by Dr Eleanor Hartley, whose eye for how Dickens constructs these effects at the level of the sentence is, frankly, a gift to any conversation about this novel.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is with us — a reader who will insist, and rightly, that we never lose sight of the individual souls inhabiting these spaces.
Daniel, let's begin with the Boffins' Bower — that extraordinary room Silas Wegg first enters.
What does Dickens do with that interior?
The Bower is one of the most precisely diagnostic interiors in Victorian fiction.
Dickens opens with a single devastating sentence — let me read it:
"It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg."
Notice the compound contradiction: luxurious and tap-room in the same breath.
That is not mere comic description — that is a class diagnosis.
The Boffins have money now — new money, sudden money — and the room shows exactly what happens when wealth arrives without the cultural apparatus to absorb it.
The drawing-room furniture sits beside the tavern settles; the flowery carpet stops dead at Mrs Boffin's footstool and gives way to sand and sawdust.
There is a literal territorial border inside one room — between aspiration and origin.
And what's so brilliant, structurally, is that Dickens gives us the room entirely through Wegg's eyes — so we're seeing new money through the eyes of someone who has absolutely none.
Wegg's admiration is comic precisely because it's genuine.
He notices, with admiring eyes, the books "ranged flat, in a row, like a galvanic battery" — and then equally, the cold joint and the pie on the compensatory shelves.
The word "compensatory" is doing extraordinary work there — it's the narrator's word, not Wegg's, slipping in to tell us exactly what the sand-and-sawdust territory is compensating for.
Dickens is conducting two conversations simultaneously — one satirical, one almost tender.
I'd want to resist the temptation to read the Bower purely as a diagram of class failure.
What Dickens seems to me to be doing — with real affection — is showing us two people who have come into wealth and simply kept on being themselves.
The carpet stops at Mrs Boffin's footstool not because she has failed socially, but because she is more comfortable in the familiar half of her own room.
That is, if you will allow it, a rather admirable form of integrity.
The novel ultimately validates the Boffins' decency far more than it does the pretensions of those who sneer at them.
I don't dispute the affection — it's genuinely there.
But the border in that room is not a private psychological fact — it is a social one, and Dickens knows it.
He goes on to note that the old-fashioned windows and crooked ceiling suggest the house had once been "a house of some mark standing alone in the country."
The Bower itself has a history of dispossession — and the Boffins are only its latest inheritors.
Let's move from private interiors to public institutions, because Dickens is equally devastating about schools.
Daniel, you've looked closely at the school Charley Hexam attends — what's happening there?
The school passage is one of the most controlled pieces of polemic in the novel, and its anger is entirely earned.
Dickens gives us the whole farce of Victorian philanthropic education in a single institution.
Young women, old in the vices of the streets, are expected to be enchanted by Little Margery — a child who lectures a miller and divides her porridge with singing birds.
The mismatch between the literature and the lives of the pupils is not accidental — it is the point.
And then Dickens reaches his verdict — let me read it:
"An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night."
The incantatory repetition of "jumbled" is not rhetorical excess — it enacts the confusion it describes.
The form mirrors the content: a system so disordered it can only be rendered as verbal chaos.
That passage is extraordinary precisely because it shifts registers mid-flight.
It opens with social satire — the absurdity of Little Margery and Thomas Twopence — and then it suddenly becomes something close to a formal experiment.
And then the Sunday scene — the "chief executioner" and his acolyte, smoothing the faces of exhausted infants — that's not satire any more.
That is something closer to horror.
Dickens lets the imagery do his arguing for him — he doesn't need to tell us the system is cruel; he shows us the boy anointing infants for a whisker.
One ought to observe, though, that Dickens reserves his real tenderness for the child in the system — Charley Hexam himself.
The satire is directed at the institution, not the pupils who are its victims.
Dickens was always more interested in what a bad system does to a specific soul than in condemning systems as such.
It is the individual moral fate that concerns him — as it always does.
From the schoolroom to the dining room — and the extraordinary figure of Lady Tippins, who almost turns political corruption into a parlour game.
Daniel, what do you make of Dickens's portrait of the Veneerings' election campaign?
Lady Tippins is doing something quite extraordinary here — she is describing the corruption of electoral democracy with absolute frankness, and calling it refreshing.
The key passage is almost breathtaking in its candour — she tells everyone she meets:

"And we are carrying on this little farce to keep up appearances, and isn't it refreshing! Then, my precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights."
Nobody knows who the Veneerings are — and nobody needs to.
In this world, a spectacular house and extravagant dinners are sufficient credentials for a parliamentary seat.
Dickens is showing us democracy as pure theatre — where the audience knows it's theatre and applauds anyway.
The voice Dickens gives Lady Tippins is a technical masterpiece — it's breathless, cumulative, and it never pauses for breath because it can't afford to.
If she stops talking, someone might ask a serious question.
Dickens renders her entire speech as free indirect discourse — we're inside her social performance as she delivers it.
And the phrase "my own Veneerings, my exclusive property" is perfectly chosen — she doesn't even pretend to treat them as people.
Lady Tippins is, of course, a superb comic creation — but I think we must be careful not to mistake Dickens's comedy for his politics.
He satirises the Veneerings not because they have purchased a parliamentary seat — that was, after all, entirely normal — but because they are hollow.
They have a house out of the Tales of the Genii — it is all surface, all show, with no substance beneath.
Dickens's charge is moral, not constitutional.
And from the social comedy of Pocket-Breaches, we come at last to the river itself — the novel's darkest and most insistent setting.
Daniel, there's a passage where John Harmon — in hiding, under an assumed identity — discovers the placard announcing his own death.
What does Dickens do with the Thames at that moment?
It's the moment where the river becomes something more than atmosphere — it becomes the novel's central image of what money does to human identity.
Harmon, in his own narration, reaches the terrible recognition — let me read it:

"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
The repetition of "same dark" is devastating — two men, interchangeable in death, disposed of in the same current.
The river doesn't care who you are — it receives murderer and victim alike, as long as both are in the way of money.
And Harmon's narration at this point has this extraordinary quality of a man watching himself from the outside.
He rushes to see his own corpse — "in a wild incautious way" — and the phrase tells us that even the rational part of him has given way.
Dickens is writing about the dissolution of identity under extreme psychological pressure — and the river is the perfect objective correlative for that dissolution.
It flows, it mixes, it obscures — it gives nothing back cleanly.
This is, I think, where the novel achieves something genuinely profound.
Harmon's predicament is not merely social — it is existential in the oldest sense.
He must decide who he is — not what class he belongs to, but what kind of man he will choose to be.
The river strips away every social identity and leaves only the naked question of character.
And the river offers one more extraordinary moment — when it holds Rogue Riderhood between life and death, and the narrator addresses him directly.
Daniel, that passage feels like a different register entirely from anything else in the novel.
It is entirely different — and its difference is itself a form of argument.
Riderhood is the novel's most purely degraded figure — a man who has sold information, informed on others, scraped existence from the river's worst leavings.
And yet Dickens refuses to let him simply die — or simply live — without confronting us with a mystery.
The narrator addresses him directly — here is the passage:
"If you are gone for good, Rogue, it is very solemn, and if you are coming back, it is hardly less so."
The solemnity is extended to a man who has done nothing to earn it — and that is precisely the point.
The river makes all lives equally strange, equally suspended — and Dickens insists we feel that, even for Rogue Riderhood.
The narrator's sudden intimacy with Riderhood — calling him "Rogue" — is one of those moments where Dickens breaks through his own ironical mode entirely.
There's the detail that those in attendance are "alike afraid to look on you and to look off you" — that suspended, helpless attention in the presence of someone neither fully alive nor fully dead.
Dickens understands that this threshold state is where the river's real meaning lives.
What strikes me here is the extraordinary democracy of that solemnity.
Dickens does not exempt even the worst of his characters from the solemn facts of mortality.
There is no sentimentality in it — he does not pretend Riderhood is better than he is.
He simply refuses to reduce any human life, however wasted, to a mere occasion for moral instruction.
That seems to me exactly the right note on which to end this section — the Thames as the novel's great leveller, the space where class and identity and mortality all converge.
We've moved from the Boffins' carpet to the dark tide, and Dickens has insisted all the way that every setting is an argument.
After the break, we'll turn to the novel's extraordinary gallery of self-made men — and the question of what, exactly, they've made themselves into.

segments.title: Character in Motion: Transformation and Redemption

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring how Dickens builds his world — the river, the dust heaps, the money that flows through everything.
In this segment, we turn to the people inside that world — and specifically to the question of how characters change, or resist changing, or are shaped before they ever get the chance.
Eleanor Hartley has been given four passages today — and they are, I think, four of the most revealing character portraits in the novel.
Eleanor, let's begin with Eugene Wrayburn — a man who seems to have been categorised before he could speak.
Yes — and that is precisely the joke, and the tragedy, that Dickens is playing with in this passage.
Eugene is recounting how his father — M. R. F., the Most Respected Father — pre-assigned a destiny to each child before they were even born.
The structure of the speech is a comic litany — each sibling presented, labelled, and then gently shown to have failed the label.
Listen to how Dickens times the punchline when he gets to the second brother.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
That last clause — 'a very shaky one' — is Dickens at his most precise.
Three words that deflate an entire institution — the church, paternal authority, the Victorian idea of providential vocation — all at once.
Eleanor is right about the comic architecture — but I'd want to push a little further on what the joke is actually doing morally.
Eugene tells this story with what he calls 'affectionate deference' toward M. R. F. — but the deference is entirely ironic, and the affection is strictly for Eugene's own amusement.
That, to me, is the defining characteristic of Eugene at this stage in the novel — he is a man who has turned his own purposelessness into an aesthetic.
He laughs at M. R. F.'s categorisations, yes. But he also lives inside them — he is the barrister who doesn't practise.
The question Dickens poses — which will not be answered until much later and at great cost — is whether Eugene's wit is armour or paralysis.
I take Edmund's point, but I'd name the paralysis differently.
What the passage actually enumerates is a class system reproducing itself through the body — the eldest inherits, the second enters the church, the third is 'pitch-forked into the Navy.'
Each son is a function, not a person. And M. R. F. declares these functions before the children can object — even before they are born.
Eugene finds this amusing because he has enough capital — cultural and actual — to float above his assigned role and call the floating irony.
The characters who don't have that luxury — Sloppy, Jenny Wren — they can't afford elegant disengagement.
And that contrast is exactly what makes Eleanor's second passage so powerful — because Jenny Wren is the absolute opposite of elegant disengagement.
Jenny has a vision — she describes celestial children who appear to her in long bright rows, dressed in white, asking a single terrible question.
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
What stops me cold every time is that refrain — the question is also a recognition.
The children don't say 'What is the matter?' They already know someone is suffering. The question is only — who is it?
And Jenny answers: it's poor me. That self-identification — spoken to a dream — is one of the most heartbreaking moments in the novel.
I find that passage almost unbearably moving — and I think it works because Dickens is doing something unusual for him there.
He gives Jenny a private interior world of grace — not one imposed by society or institution, but self-generated from pain.
The celestial children are not a reward for virtue. They come to her because she suffers — that is the whole of their criterion.
There's a genuinely theological quality to that — the idea that suffering itself is a form of address to something beyond the world.
Dickens rarely earns that register without sentimentality. Here, I think he does — because Jenny's suffering is never prettified.
I won't argue with the tenderness — but the passage also tells us something very specific about what Jenny's daily life actually is.
She says the children she actually saw as a child — the neighbours' children — made her tremble with their shrill noises, and mocked her.
So the vision is not just spiritual comfort — it is the only community that has ever treated her with dignity.
A child who has been beaten and mocked and chilled has to go outside the material world entirely to find welcome. That is a social indictment, not just a lyrical vision.
I want to hold those two tones together — Daniel's anger and Edmund's tenderness — and move to a very different register.
Because there's a passage about Sloppy in his new black suit that is, on the surface, pure comic relief — and I want to argue it's doing something quite precise.
Rokesmith has commissioned a tailor with instructions to conceal the buttons — to make Sloppy look, essentially, like a gentleman.
The tailor fails magnificently. Dickens writes that Sloppy stood before the Council —
"a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The Argus myth — the hundred-eyed giant — is gloriously absurd applied to trouser buttons.
But Argus was also the guardian, the watcher — and there's a sly implication that Sloppy's body is resisting the disguise, asserting its own presence, refusing to be gentrified.
That's a beautiful reading — and it connects directly to what I was saying about Jenny.
The benevolent characters in this novel — Boffin, Rokesmith — try to help by dressing Sloppy up, making him legible to polite society.
But the body won't cooperate. His trousers hitch up. His sleeves bag at the elbows. The gulf at his waistband refuses to close.
You can dress poverty in black broadcloth, but the underlying form insists on being seen.
I'd offer a gentler version of that same reading.
The comedy here is warm — it's affectionate, not contemptuous. Dickens is not mocking Sloppy. He's celebrating the irrepressibility of the thing itself.
The 'artistic taste of some unknown hatter' who furnishes the fluted hatband — that phrase is beautifully double-edged.
The hatter has artistic taste, apparently — it's just taste of a rather wholesale kind. Dickens is laughing with Sloppy, not at him.
And then — from that comic warmth — Dickens moves us somewhere entirely different, in the passage that has stayed with me longest from this set.
It's the scene where Bradley Headstone is pursuing Eugene Wrayburn along the river — skulking on the opposite bank as the boat moves under the trees.
And then the sun goes down. Dickens writes —
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
That 'as we say' is the stroke that makes it extraordinary.
The narrator steps forward and invokes a collective moral memory — we all know this proverb, this dread — and then embeds it in a landscape.
The red light is not metaphor — it is evidence. And it has not yet happened. The violence is still ahead.
That passage is, I think, one of the great examples of Dickens using landscape not as decoration but as moral atmosphere.
Bradley Headstone is at this point all suppressed will and murderous intent — and the landscape answers him, as though nature itself is registering the moral temperature.
What interests me is the word 'guiltily.' The blood hasn't been shed yet — but the guilt, in a sense, is already present in Bradley's heart.
Dickens is making the landscape read the interior of the character — which is a remarkable thing to do with light on a river.
Edmund is right about the moral register — though I'd add a dimension he might resist slightly.
Bradley Headstone is one of the most interesting characters in the novel precisely because his violence is not random cruelty — it is the product of a specific social position.
He has clawed his way up from poverty through education, only to find that a man like Eugene — effortless, leisured, idle — can still hold him in contempt.
The red landscape isn't only guilt — it's also rage. The rage of a man who achieved everything the system promised, and found the promise hollow.
That image — blood mounting to heaven before it's been shed — seems to me a perfect closing note for this segment.
We've moved from Eugene's polished detachment, through Jenny's pain-born visions, through Sloppy's gleaming, indomitable buttons — and arrived at this terrible red light on the river.
What connects them, I think, is exactly what Eleanor, Edmund, and Daniel have each been tracing — the question of what a person is before the world has finished making them, or destroying them.
After the break, we'll turn to the institutions — the law, philanthropy, the social machinery that surrounds these characters and, as Daniel would say, produces them.

segments.title: Laughter and Darkness: Comedy in a Novel of Critique

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see what makes it tick.
Today's segment asks a question that sits at the very heart of this novel: how does Dickens hold darkness and comedy in the same hand?
Because Our Mutual Friend is gothic and satirical and tender, often within the same paragraph — and that tonal balancing act is, I'd argue, where the novel's genius most clearly lives.
With me to unpick it are three extraordinary readers of this novel.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about the architecture of fiction — how sentences are built, how images carry weight, how structure shapes meaning.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist — a novelist of character, conscience, and the individual soul under pressure.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees in every Dickens scene a precise anatomy of how class power distributes itself — who gains, who suffers, and why.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with a moment in the very first chapter that I think perfectly crystallises what we're talking about.
Yes — and it's a moment so brief it could almost slip past you, which is exactly how Dickens wants it.
Gaffer Hexam has just pulled something from the river — from a corpse, though Dickens never says so directly at this point — and it's money.
And then comes this extraordinary little ritual — which Dickens sets up with a sentence so perfectly timed it could be from a piece of music.
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once, — 'for luck,' he hoarsely said — before he put it in his pocket."
Three beats: chinked, blew, spat — each one exactly alike, building a rhythm that is almost ceremonial.
It's comic — the spitting, the hoarse little word 'for luck' — and yet there's something genuinely chilling underneath it.
Dickens has given us the whole novel's tonal signature in a single paragraph: the grotesque and the funny are not opposites here — they're the same thing.
Eleanor is right about the craft — but I'd want to press on what that ritual actually reveals about Gaffer as a moral creature.
Because 'for luck' is doing something very specific.
It is a superstition — a tiny prayer, spoken hoarsely over money drawn from a dead man.
Gaffer has not lost his conscience entirely — that is the tragedy, and the comedy at once.
He feels he needs luck — which implies he senses, however dimly, that what he does may not deserve it.
The comedy is not satirical in the Swiftian sense — it is the comedy of self-deception, which is always the most revealing kind.
I take Edmund's point, but I think the comedy here operates on a different register as well — a structural one.
Notice what Gaffer does first: he washes his arms over the side of the boat.
His arms are wet and dirty — the text is precise about that — and he washes the money too.
The money comes from death, is cleaned in the very river that produced the corpse, and then pocketed.
Dickens has written — in one paragraph — the entire logic of capital accumulation in this novel.
Wealth is extracted from the most wretched circumstances, ritually purified, and placed where it cannot be questioned.
The comedy — the spitting, the hoarse little invocation — is Dickens's way of making that visible without making it a lecture.
Daniel, that's exactly what I mean about the image carrying a chapter's meaning — and I think we can see the same tonal range operating very differently later in the novel.
Mrs Boffin's proposal to adopt a child and name him John Harmon is one of those moments that could so easily tip into sentimentality — and Dickens knows it.
What saves it is the precision of the comedy before it: she 'pulled his nearest ear' in response to his philosophy — a detail so domestically exact that it earns the tenderness that follows.
And then she says something that is quietly devastating in its generosity.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
'Say it's only a whim' — she adds that, as if apologising for her own goodness.
That qualification is where the comedy and the tenderness meet — she's embarrassed by her own impulse toward grace, and that embarrassment makes it absolutely real.
And it is real — which is the point, I think, that Daniel's reading sometimes risks obscuring.
Mrs Boffin is not a function of the novel's economic critique — she is a good woman.
The proposal to adopt an orphan, to give the dead boy's name to a living child — that is an act of moral imagination responding to death with care rather than mere acquisition.
Dickens believed in goodness as a fact — not as an ideology — and Mrs Boffin is his evidence.
I don't dispute that Mrs Boffin is drawn with great warmth — Dickens clearly loves her.
But notice what the passage turns on: the money has 'come to them' because John Harmon is 'past all benefit of it.'
The inheritance is the condition of the generosity — without the fortune built on old Harmon's miserable dust-heaps, Mrs Boffin has no orphan to adopt and no name to bestow.
Dickens is tender about this — he doesn't expose Mrs Boffin — but the structure of the scene does it for him, quietly and without malice.
Redemption in this novel is always funded — and the comedy of the ear-pulling, the whimsy of 'say it's only a whim,' softens the harder truth beneath it.
Which brings us to what I think is the most technically dazzling comic scene in the novel — Bella's kneeling before Mr Boffin near the end.
The setup is almost farcical: Bella hands the baby to John with the air of someone delegating minor administrative duties, then drops to her knees beside Boffin.
And what she says is pure Dickens — it's a speech act that is simultaneously a retraction, a declaration, and a comic riff.
"Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!"
That word 'please' — repeated, insistent, childlike — does something remarkable: it makes the most emotionally loaded revelation in the plot feel light.
And the laughter in the scene — 'an exultant ringing laugh' — is not separate from the truth being spoken; it is the form in which the truth arrives.
There is something almost Shakespearean in that scene — the disguise lifted, the truth told with a laugh rather than a confession.
Bella has been tested, and she has passed — and the comedy is the reward for moral seriousness rather than a retreat from it.
What strikes me most is the phrase 'his delighted face' — Boffin can't keep the performance going against her joy.
That is the novel's deepest argument, I think: goodness is irresistible to goodness — and no amount of theatrical miserliness can suppress it for long.
I find this scene extraordinary — and also, I confess, slightly troubling — for the same reason.
Bella's transformation — from a girl who frankly prizes money to a woman capable of this radiant, kneeling grace — is the novel's central redemption arc.
But notice what makes the revelation possible: it is Boffin who designed the performance, Boffin who managed Bella's moral education from above.
The comedy of 'please' — all that light, ringing exultation — masks the fact that Bella's redemption was administered to her by the wealthy benefactor.
Dickens finds this beautiful, and his comedy makes us find it beautiful — which is, if you'll allow me, the most ideologically effective thing this novel does.
Three readings — a craft argument, a moral argument, and a structural argument — and yet all three seem to agree that the comedy is doing real, serious work.

From Gaffer's chink and spit over dead men's money, to Mrs Boffin's pulled ear and bashful whim, to Bella's ringing, kneeling laugh — Dickens keeps finding ways to make darkness bearable without making it dishonest.
Coming up: we turn to the river itself — what it holds, what it releases, and why Dickens keeps returning to its surface throughout the novel.

segments.title: Closing: Dust to Life—Dickens's Vision of Renewal

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great currents running through Our Mutual Friend — the river, the dust, the money, the masks people wear.
Before we close, I want to ask each of our guests one final question.
What does Dickens ultimately offer his readers in this novel — is it a vision of renewal, or something more complicated than that?
Edmund, you've been our guide to moral character throughout — let's begin with you.
Thank you. I think the vision Dickens offers is not renewal in any programmatic sense — not a reformed society or a corrected institution.
What he offers is something far more intimate: the spectacle of goodness persisting, unfashionably, against every pressure to conform.
Think of the Boffins. The novel gives us this extraordinarily tender little moment between them.
Mr Boffin says to his wife:
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And the narrator adds — with that inimitable Dickensian double edge — that this was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations.
They sit together, as Dickens puts it, 'a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
Hopelessly — and yet wholly enviable. That is Dickens's deepest moral note in this novel.
Edmund's reading is beautiful, and I won't quarrel with the tenderness of that scene.
But I'd argue that 'hopelessly Unfashionable' is doing political work as much as moral work.
The Boffins are rich — suddenly, absurdly rich — and yet they cannot purchase the social legitimacy that the novel's fashionable world demands.
Dickens is showing us that the market in status is rigged — that accumulated capital alone cannot buy you into the ruling class's self-regard.
Their goodness excludes them. Which tells us something sharp about what fashionability actually requires.
And then there's Miss Wren — Jenny Wren — who closes the loop on justice in a way no institution in this novel ever manages.
She applies pepper to Fledgeby's plasters, and she frames it as a moral reckoning — listen to this:
'I think the young man's tricks and manners make a claim upon his friends for a little pepper?'
The courts won't touch Fledgeby. The law won't touch him. Jenny Wren does — with pepper and a silent laugh.
What I keep returning to, in this final question about renewal, is how Dickens handles interiority — or rather, refuses to handle it directly.
The passage about Lizzie and Eugene is a perfect example of his method at its most controlled.
The narrator says of Lizzie:
'Lizzie sat so still, that one could not have said wherein the fact of her manner being troubled was expressed; and yet one could not have doubted it.'
Look at the architecture of that sentence — the double negation, the almost legal precision of 'wherein the fact of her manner being troubled was expressed.'
Dickens doesn't tell us she is troubled. He tells us we could not have said how we knew — and yet we could not have doubted it.
That is the technique of renewal in miniature — knowledge that arrives without explanation, feeling that precedes language.
Dickens trusts the reader to feel what cannot be said. And that trust — that mutual faith between writer and reader — is perhaps the real renewal the novel enacts.
Eleanor's point about trust strikes me as exactly right — and it connects, I think, to what Daniel was saying about justice.
The institutions in this novel are largely bankrupt. Dickens knows that. But he does not despair, and he does not reach for abstraction.
He reaches instead for the particular — a man's simple pleasure in the woman he married, a girl's still, troubled face, a doll's dressmaker armed with pepper.
These are not solutions. But they are, in the deepest sense, affirmations — of character, of love, of the quietly defiant will to go on.
And Dickens earned those affirmations, I think — because he never flinched from showing what they were up against.
Our Mutual Friend is one of the bleakest anatomies of a money society ever written in English.
And yet — and this is the thing I keep returning to — the light that gets through is all the more extraordinary for the darkness around it.
Dust to life — that was Dickens's great wager in this novel, and I think the three of you have shown us precisely how he made good on it.
A goodness that is hopelessly unfashionable. A trouble that cannot be located but cannot be doubted. A pepper pot wielded as an instrument of justice.
My deepest thanks to Dr Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Dr Daniel Rosen — it has been a privilege and a pleasure.
And thank you, as ever, for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself

      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must

c5:p121.text:
It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious
      amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg. There
      were two wooden settles by the fire, one on either side of it, with a
      corresponding table before each. On one of these tables, the eight volumes
      were ranged flat, in a row, like a galvanic battery; on the other, certain
      squat case-bottles of inviting appearance seemed to stand on tiptoe to
      exchange glances with Mr Wegg over a front row of tumblers and a basin of
      white sugar. On the hob, a kettle steamed; on the hearth, a cat reposed.
      Facing the fire between the settles, a sofa, a footstool, and a little
      table, formed a centrepiece devoted to Mrs Boffin. They were garish in
      taste and colour, but were expensive articles of drawing-room furniture
      that had a very odd look beside the settles and the flaring gaslight
      pendent from the ceiling. There was a flowery carpet on the floor; but,
      instead of reaching to the fireside, its glowing vegetation stopped short
      at Mrs Boffin’s footstool, and gave place to a region of sand and sawdust.
      Mr Wegg also noticed, with admiring eyes, that, while the flowery land
      displayed such hollow ornamentation as stuffed birds and waxen fruits
      under glass-shades, there were, in the territory where vegetation ceased,
      compensatory shelves on which the best part of a large pie and likewise of
      a cold joint were plainly discernible among other solids. The room itself
      was large, though low; and the heavy frames of its old-fashioned windows,
      and the heavy beams in its crooked ceiling, seemed to indicate that it had
      once been a house of some mark standing alone in the country.
c5:p121.summary: Wegg observes the Bower's bizarrely hybrid interior: elegant drawing-room furniture mixed with tavern-style settles, books displayed like a battery, foodstuffs openly arranged, and a carpet that gives way to sand and sawdust, revealing the Boffins' uncertain class status and mixture of fashion and comfort.
c5:p121.best_quote: It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg.

c18:p1.text:
It was a school for all ages, and for both sexes. The latter were kept
      apart, and the former were partitioned off into square assortments. But,
      all the place was pervaded by a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil
      was childish and innocent. This pretence, much favoured by the
      lady-visitors, led to the ghastliest absurdities. Young women old in the
      vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves
      enthralled by the good child’s book, the Adventures of Little Margery, who
      resided in the village cottage by the mill; severely reproved and morally
      squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty; divided her
      porridge with singing birds; denied herself a new nankeen bonnet, on the
      ground that the turnips did not wear nankeen bonnets, neither did the
      sheep who ate them; who plaited straw and delivered the dreariest orations
      to all comers, at all sorts of unseasonable times. So, unwieldy young
      dredgers and hulking mudlarks were referred to the experiences of Thomas
      Twopence, who, having resolved not to rob (under circumstances of uncommon
      atrocity) his particular friend and benefactor, of eighteenpence,
      presently came into supernatural possession of three and sixpence, and
      lived a shining light ever afterwards. (Note, that the benefactor came to
      no good.) Several swaggering sinners had written their own biographies in
      the same strain; it always appearing from the lessons of those very
      boastful persons, that you were to do good, not because it  was  good, but
      because you were to make a good thing of it. Contrariwise, the adult
      pupils were taught to read (if they could learn) out of the New Testament;
      and by dint of stumbling over the syllables and keeping their bewildered
      eyes on the particular syllables coming round to their turn, were as
      absolutely ignorant of the sublime history, as if they had never seen or
      heard of it. An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a
      school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white,
      jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night. And particularly
      every Sunday night. For then, an inclined plane of unfortunate infants
      would be handed over to the prosiest and worst of all the teachers with
      good intentions, whom nobody older would endure. Who, taking his stand on
      the floor before them as chief executioner, would be attended by a
      conventional volunteer boy as executioner’s assistant. When and where it
      first became the conventional system that a weary or inattentive infant in
      a class must have its face smoothed downward with a hot hand, or when and
      where the conventional volunteer boy first beheld such system in
      operation, and became inflamed with a sacred zeal to administer it,
      matters not. It was the function of the chief executioner to hold forth,
      and it was the function of the acolyte to dart at sleeping infants,
      yawning infants, restless infants, whimpering infants, and smooth their
      wretched faces; sometimes with one hand, as if he were anointing them for
      a whisker; sometimes with both hands, applied after the fashion of
      blinkers. And so the jumble would be in action in this department for a
      mortal hour; the exponent drawling on to My Dearert Childerrenerr, let us
      say, for example, about the beautiful coming to the Sepulchre; and
      repeating the word Sepulchre (commonly used among infants) five hundred
      times, and never once hinting what it meant; the conventional boy
      smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole
      hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes,
      whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in
      High Market for the purpose.
c18:p1.summary: The narrator satirizes the school's pretense of innocence, the unsuitable moral literature forced on corrupt pupils, and the brutal Sunday school system where teachers violently 'smooth' inattentive children.
c18:p1.best_quote: An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.
